utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellency. And good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up, for the benefit of the witness, 65 ter 1118.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] This is Exhibit P3758, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this letter? I apologise. I showed you this yesterday. Can you please bear with me a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Actually, I need 1D0568.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1D05608.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recall this decree with which you governed the treatment of the abandoned land and agricultural machinery that protected the rights of their owners? Maybe you can recall this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tackled this issue slightly yesterday. I really cannot remember each individual enactment at this moment. But, yes, it is true, we did regulate the cases of abandoned land, property, and the protection of their ownerships.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to remind both the Chamber and the participants of the testimony of Colm Doyle who, on the 16th of August, 1992, informed us that various certificates were being issued on gift deeds issued to individuals. On the 16th of August, I issued an enactment on the basis of which all these certificates on giving these kind of properties as gifts were rendered null and void. And, in addition, the prime minister issued this decree regulating the use of the abandoned properties and the protection of their rights, and I need D101. Maybe that's not the correct document, but, nevertheless, it puts a ban on forcible relocation of population, and all these enactments are rendered null and void. Is it possible that we admit this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we -- I have no problem admitting this document, but this is not the time for you to make your submission. Just ask questions to the witness. And you will have ample time to submit your interpretation of all the evidence, as you see them. Let's continue. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] As Exhibit D2246, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, if I fulfil 98 bis rule, then I will not have enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps Dr. Karadzic is saying that if he's successful in his Rule 98 bis motion, there won't be any occasion for him to offer evidence in the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was convinced that I am good at English humour, but it seems I am still an apprentice in that area. Can we now have document 1D04192. It's already been admitted into evidence as 1D1671.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please focus on this enactment issued by the Ministry of the Interior on the 17th of April, which is the period where I -- when I didn't have any statehood position. So you can see that even at that times efforts were made towards issuing warning to public security stations to the fact that there were misappropriations of both movable and immovable property, and in addition to that, the ministry is being ordered as to what they're supposed to do. Do you recall that? because you were at the head of the government at that time and that was one of your tasks.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this, because this is a document issued by the ministry. I had no awareness of this. But there were general instructions that strict abidance by the rules should be observed with regard to everybody's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, pause between the questions and answers, please. Interpreters are having difficult time to catch up with your speed. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked Professor Djeric - and we're talking about the 17th of April when I had no official function - this was done by the government without any instructions from me whatsoever. It was their own initiative, and you confirmed that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document issued by the Ministry of the Interior. In other words, this is something that they were obliged to do based on the Law on the Government. So there's no need for me to confirm anything. This is a document from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that was the proper procedure to be followed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because our concept and our vision was that everybody's right should be protected and not jeopardized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please now have 65 ter 28. It's the minute of meeting of the Assembly session held on 24th to 26th July ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 14 in Serbian, and 17 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, I am again addressing the Assembly. And please let us look at the paragraph in the middle, which begins: "I must say that the Serb people, whose Orthodox nature has kept them from being inhumane, have found a number of traitors among themselves, inhumane people who are committing inhumane acts, the ones that we shall try and punish by the law. From the most severe acts to the smallest. The most severe acts are the rarest, while the smallest ones are the more frequent, as shown by the statistics. Such as robbery, unlawful acquiring of property, et cetera. All of that is a sequence of a terrible war, the most horrible among civil wars. In essence, it is not a civil war because it is an interethnic and religious war. I can say that the Serbs have stayed away from other people's property, especially away from the property of the members of other nations and ethnic groups. War has changed some people so much that there are individuals among whom are those keen on other people's property, both Muslim and Serb property. Here we have great political problems. It is an immense blow to our soldiers' morale, which is otherwise excellent, but, in any case, this is something that hurts them while they are fighting. There are robberies and crimes being done behind their backs ..." Are you familiar with these views which were not only mine but they were shared by the entire leadership?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know about this, although I wouldn't agree with you concerning the perception of the war itself. It was a civil war that had some ingredients of interethnic and interreligious war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you need to put a pause after Mr. Djeric's answer as well. Yes, repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was in relation to what I was talking about, from 24 to 26 July, was whether Professor Djeric was familiar with this view, which was not only my view but the one shared by the entire leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I believe that the transcript has properly recorded Professor Djeric's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you -- after Professor Djeric has given his answer, you started asking some questions, which was overlapped with the translation of Mr. Djeric's answer. So that part is not noted in the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also, I'm not sure whether everything is recorded. You, Professor, agreed, didn't you, that this was our view, with the exception that you don't think that the nature of the war is exactly as I qualified it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is what I said. If you want me to repeat, I can say that what you said were the views of the leadership and the politicians at that time. The only thing I would disagree with you about was the nature of the war. I said that that was a civil war that had some ingredients in it of interethnic and religious war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that, do you mean that Abdic was a different Muslim, and that we had Muslims in our army as well, which makes the religious component not being the primary component?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that the religious component was the principal one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at 65 ter 4214, which is P456, I think. Your Excellencies, while we are waiting, with all due respect, I wish to remind you that for KDZ192 I was allotted four hours; and for this witness, who headed the government and held hundreds of sessions of the government and the Presidency and the Council for National Security and issued thousands or -- 1.000-odd memos, I was also allotted four hours. I think this is not enough for any of us. Could we please see page 17 in Serbian and 15 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's at about the middle of the passage beginning where it says "I have to say ..." in the second paragraph, where the cursor is now. So perhaps the 15th line from above towards the right margin. "It absolutely has to serve the front and establishing the borders." Have you located that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show to the professor with the cursor where we are; it's about the 15th line from the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean this that begins with the words "I can say"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. Rather, "I have to say," about ten lines down on the same page.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I have noticed it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. It says: "I must say that it often happened that some municipal officials behaved unlawfully up to the point of necessitating their arrest and punishment. This is something that we, as the Assembly, must point out and perhaps even punish a find a way for the Presidency to take a stand in such matters between two sessions of the Assembly. Namely, we should consider ourselves lucky that there have not been any executions so far, but in future, there will have to be arrests and punishment. This Assembly, as the legislative body and the body whose duty it is to protect the legality, will have to note this and give us authorisation, even if we do not declare a state of war, in order to straighten things out in certain municipalities which are of vital importance. We will have to use vigorous measures." Do you remember that in our system there were many residual elements of the previous system and you could not replace anyone, you could only appeal to their deputies to replace him or ask him to submit his resignation? Any villain, I mean.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I remember. I talked about that yesterday. The power of the local authorities and the consequences which followed. I would say in a positive sense as well that was part of the self-management system during the time that the authorities functioned well. That provided freedom to people. They could express themselves freely and so on. It was a time when people came to love the authorities. And this is the territory where people love authorities, they love power, and they tend to want to be in power. I have to say this unwillingly, though - where the culture of violence is quite prominent, and it takes quite some time for it to allow arguments and recognition of the other side to become prominent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see page 57 in Serbian in this document and 53 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this to come up, would you agree, Mr. Djeric, that in addition to the weaknesses that can be attributed to the mentality and the system in 1990, the people who came in power were those who had been marginal previously, or they had been in the opposition, and they did not have sufficient knowledge or expertise to fulfil their role as the people who are in power and to do it properly on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm this. I would even say that it was not a lack of knowledge, but, rather, complete ignorance, because during the political changes which occurred, the people who came to the fore were people who were braver. I suppose it was just such an era. And those with more knowledge were fewer, so courage was decisive. And it's not characteristic only for our region. I mean, for Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was the period of transition. The gentlemen sitting here are very well aware of the cases of Armenia, Georgia, Northern and Southern Ossetia, and so on and so forth. It -- this is transition symptom. Or how should I call it? It's something specific that happens when the systems are changed and went from a society where everything is commandeered, you have to move into a democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please scroll down the page in Serbian. And the line begins with the words, "but profiteers are working or the presidents of municipalities are disobedient." Can you please have a look.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please scroll down the page in Serbian a little bit. It's perhaps ten lines from the bottom or the -- 12 lines from the bottom. It begins with: "Either the profiteers are active or the presidents of municipalities are disobedient."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you found that, Professor? It's a bit above the cursor.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the font is small, and I cannot really see well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us collapse the English version so that the witness can follow better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see it? It's perhaps ten or 12 lines from the bottom. 13 lines from the bottom. Either the profiteers are doing their work or --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... or the presidents of the municipalities are disobedient." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So can you see it's the same. This is the Assembly session from September. Excuse me. The 14th and the 15th of September, 1992, held in Bijeljina. Probably here it says: "Either the profiteers are doing their work" - these are my words - "or the presidents of the municipalities are disobedient. Who is the president of the municipality here in Bijeljina? Is Zlatko present? Once again, this man will not listen. He was ordered by the government that two short-wave transmitters should be moved to Yugoslavia and two should remain here, and certainly then the greatest part of the world would be covered. He won't do that. And the police nowhere wants to arrest. The judges won't put anyone to trial. There are no reports. And Father Savo said well what this is about. Are we the hosts here in this house? Are we responsible leaders of our people or not? We cannot follow as if we did not care. Everything is important. Everything is significant. We have to establish central organs of power. We have to establish central police that will come here and arrest people. And we have to move police from Bijeljina to Doboj and from Doboj to Bijeljina." So, do you remember that it was not easy to arrest anyone because people were connected? They were relatives or friends, people who had positions in the ground, and there was a lack of professionalism.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. These were the biggest problems that we had. The problems of what was happening on the ground in local areas was very difficult and very slow. Implementing our authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that in late July when we needed to arrest the Yellow Wasps we had to engage the special police brigade, and in order to do the arrests in Bijeljina and Brcko, we even requested from Panic to send the special forces, and he did send them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the use of police, I do not know much about that. I was not in the know, because the command and use of the police forces was a part of your jurisdiction, so I cannot say anything about that. But as for the Yellow Wasps, I can just say that I remember from what was being said, because I was not present or directly involved, but I heard that the special unit, the assault unit of the police, was used to disperse the Yellow Wasps. And the reason was, as people said, that the Yellow Wasps had overstepped the limit, that they had stopped a minister. It was Minister Ostojic. And allegedly they forced him to graze grass in a field. This is what the rumours were. And that was why this particular police unit was used. This is what I heard. I was not an eye-witness, so I don't really know, but this is what reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you have had half an hour that we allowed you to have for today. That means you have had about five hours and ten minutes by now. Given the circumstances, the Chamber will give you additional ten minutes. I would like you to wrap up your cross-examination in ten minutes now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I skipped many topics that I could deal with with other witnesses, but with this witness I have to cover our attitude to the camps for the prisoners of war and the arrival of 400 civilians from Bratunac to Pale, where the seat of government bodies was. The crisis about that. It would really be detrimental if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we have given our ruling. You'll have ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, would you agree with me that the Wasps turned against Ostojic because the government turned against them, so they wanted to demonstrate their force?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot assert that. I cannot make such an assertion because I really do not know that. I mean, whether they turned against the authorities, it's something I cannot assert. Perhaps can you say that on the basis of some other information and knowledge that you have. What was Ostojic doing there? I mean, he was a minister in the government. I have no idea. Perhaps he was passing through. Maybe he was there on official business. Maybe he was going in the direction of Serbia or returning from there. This is something I do not know. Simply, that's not all clear to me. So I cannot be very explicit about this incident. I don't know that. I just told you what I heard. It's possible that someone turned the whole incident into a banal affair. Again, it's something I don't know. I'm just telling you what I heard, what reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Just for your information: On his way to Belgrade, Ostojic was supposed to find information about the Yellow Wasps and then convey that to me, but they learned that and then they maltreated him. But, never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't know how long he was going to go on for. It's stopped now, but it's not appropriate for the -- for Mr. Karadzic to be educating the witness on matters. He is supposed to be eliciting information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just said that my idea was to inform the witness about this. But it really doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, I have just so much time left to remind you of the crisis that you had to resolve in the absence of all other officials and, to that end, can we please have a look at what happened in the month of May, when 400 people were transported to Pale from Bratunac. First of all, can you confirm that it is correct that Deronjic or anyone else never informed you about the combat which was ongoing in Glogova village, nor did they inform you, nor are you certain to this day, that these people were indeed from Glogova.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm all that. I have said earlier that I have no idea about that. I don't even know who Deronjic is, if you understand me. I don't even know that there was any combat going on there. I didn't know anything about that at all. The first time I faced all these issues was here at ICTY, I believe in the Krajisnik case, so not even who these people were, Drenova, or this particular gentleman, this is something I don't know. I just know that I learned two days later when these people had been brought to Pale. I was the only one who was present in Pale of the high-ranking officials, and these people had been brought there two days earlier. They were in an agricultural co-operative building, an old building it was, or perhaps a cultural centre, that was where they were held. And accidently -- actually, I mean, from my escort, from my driver, I learned this. They warned me. They said, Prime minister, are you aware, because no one has informed you, that some people have been brought here from Bratunac and there's many of them? They're being held down there. And they told me that people were being mistreated and that it was at a point where they could even be killed or crimes could be committed, and it was a matter of seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you then asked to be informed, and you received information that these Muslims wanted you to allow them to pass on to Sarajevo, and you then ordered for trucks with tarpaulins to be provided so that they would be allowed to pass through the Muslim territory in the direction of Visoko. And you also informed the municipality through which they needed to pass; I mean Ilijas. You informed them to prepare for that and to make sure that nothing would happen and that no one would shoot at them. Is all this correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I did not inform Ilijas. I did not trouble myself about that. The commissions did that, and the police. So it wasn't me personally who dealt with that. The only thing I did was I wanted to save these people that very moment. This was a matter of seconds, and, therefore, I did not want to leave it up to anyone else. I took the responsibility onto myself and I requested personally, directly, to see these people, to see what they wanted, and that their will was taken into consideration, because to return them it would make no sense. Have you to take on the responsibility. So I requested that their will had to be taken into account and that promptly all these people had to be saved. So this is what I can say here now. And to this day, it's not clear to me how this happened, who did that, what that was all about, that these people were simply brought to the seat of the democratic government. I don't understand that to this day, but this is something I can say nothing about. I can just say that we did everything that we could to save these people, and there was simply not enough time to think about any other options or alternatives or the like. The idea was to offer them what they wanted, they made their choice, and that was how it all ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that it would be inhumane and also illegal if, against their will, you returned them to the combat zone, the zone of the combat that was ongoing in Bratunac at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't have done that ever, either now or at that time. That would be an abuse of those people. Because there was high likelihood that they would not fare well. That would never even cross my mind to do something like that. I was doing everything in order to protect the freedom and the lives of these people. So that was the primary goal at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last topic that I have enough time to deal with is the question of prisoner exchanges. Do you agree that during the first days of the war a lot of prisoners were taken on both sides? Also, personal favours were being done. And perhaps money was even taken for exchanges. And then, on the 8th of May, the government passed a decision establishing a central commission and that municipalities also had their own commissions for the exchange of prisoners, bodies, et cetera. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government regulated this question at a very early stage. The government adopted certain instructions for prisoner exchanges and took care of other things as well, as far as institutionalisation was concerned. A prisoner exchange commission was established. However, there was some abuse there. Civilians were brought in, pretending to be prisoners of war. This particularly happened in Sarajevo, but elsewhere as well. It turned into a business, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was not done by the legal authorities.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by the legal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Private individuals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I said that it was that kind of business, it couldn't be the government that would be running it. Private individuals shouldn't be doing it either, unless it's a question of abuse.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1088 has already been admitted. I don't have time to call that up. Can I please ask that we look at the transcript from Stanisic/Zupljanin. Page 2459. Lines 1 through 7. 65 ter 22479. I believe it's not part of the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the subject. Did our authorities make any distinctions as far as criminal prosecution was concerned? Was there any differences in terms of background, ethnic and religious? I'll read it out in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page is not right. 2549, that's what I need. 2459.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out. [In English] "Four, paragraph 2. Please read it. "It --" [Interpretation] Now it's being read out. [In English] "'It was pointed out that the priority for both the national service and the crime investigation service, that's the MUP is to detect war crimes, provide documentation and file criminal reports, documents also provided for war crimes committed by Serbs.'" [Interpretation] Line 6, your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again the page is wrong. 2459. 2459.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is what you say: "I already mentioned that." [In English] "I already mentioned that. No distinction was drawn. All crimes had to be prosecuted." [Interpretation] That's it. That's your answer in line 6. So is that correct; namely, that the authorities did not discriminate in any way as far as the origin of war criminals was concerned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities could not have acted otherwise, if we look at the constitution and anything else. So there were no legal grounds for this, or there was no other reason for people to be treated differently. Everyone had to be treated in accordance with the law. If there would be violations, that would be a violation. Illegal behaviour, it would have to be punished. That's what I said then, and I spoke about that at length yesterday, and I'm dealing with it today again. And I advocated -- I persistently advocated the following: All of those who went beyond certain boundaries had to be punished. You did see that at a very early stage the government adopted all necessary documents for that, and the government asked for it to be established whether crimes had been committed, whether there had been inhumane behaviour towards the civilian population, towards prisoners. The government wanted that to be established and punished, if that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now it's time for you to put your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I wanted to say, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't have time, Professor Djeric, to show something from the Official Gazette, a list. I can deal with -- I can deal with this with some other witness. The government itself submitted over 700 pieces of legislation to the Assembly. And the government, Presidency, and Assembly, together during those seven months while you were prime minister, over 1.000 pieces of legislation were adopted. Do you agree, Professor Djeric, that during these three and a half years of war we had at least five prime ministers, or, rather, five governments, and I think six ministers of the interior as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, once I left, I had less interest in the government and these changes. Now, how many governments and how many ministers there were even with the best of goodwill, I could not remember. The times were difficult and I really cannot tell you. I cannot say how many changes took place. But it is correct that there were changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the last question, may I jog your memory. It was you; then after you, it was Vladimir Lukic; then after Vladimir Lukic; it was Dusko -- or, rather, Dusan Kozic; then after Dusan Kozic, it was Rajko Kasagic; after Rajko Kasagic, it was Gojko Klickovic. Five prime ministers in three and a half years; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that actually the last one served two terms, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'm sorry we didn't have more time to present the vast body of work of the government, although they basically had no proper conditions for working. Thank you for everything you did in the government, and thank you for all.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to thank Their Honours, the gentleman from the Prosecution, and all of you for --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, sir. There will be an opportunity for you to do that, but the Court was about to ask, I presume, if I had any additional questions in response to some of the questions that Mr. Karadzic, and I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Mr. Djeric. I wanted to ask you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yeah, good morning. I wanted to ask you some questions in connection with your -- with some of your testimony yesterday, around transcript page 27936, addressing the issue of the extent to which the government was cut off from communications. First of all, just a quick clarifying question. I believe you indicated that the government was located up at the top of the hill in Jahorina. By contrast, was Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Koljevic, were they down in the hill, in Pale?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The government was at the Bistrica hotel at an altitude of some 1600, 1700 metres. The mountain is about 2.000 metres. That's its peak. And everybody else was in Pale. Pale is about 800 metres. And the distance involved is about 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about some of the forms of communication that you were or were not referring to when you indicated that the government was cut off for a period of time. First of all, Mr. Djeric, were you aware of the intricacies of the military communication system designed to relay information from the field up through the chain of command to the highest echelons of military command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as military communications are concerned, I didn't know about that. They were used by the military; right? I mean, we could not rely on that, you see. When I spoke about communications, I said explicitly yesterday our PTT communications were interrupted by headquarters in Sarajevo. I'm talking about the civilian telecommunications system. Its centre was in Sarajevo. And we were on Mount Jahorina and we were cut off. That's as far as telecommunications are concerned. Now, as far as other communications are concerned - roads, namely - you know that this is a theatre of war, and quite simply, you could not travel through certain areas, so you could not tour the area. So, you know, you could not just travel and tour different areas. That could take place only later, say, by helicopter, if the top political leadership managed to get helicopters from the military. And then, perhaps, people could travel. You could travel, say, to Herzegovina or Krajina. But this was a few months into the conflict. Now, these helicopters, I remember they were used exclusively at the request of the top leadership. I assume it was parliament. When Assembly meetings were supposed to be held, then members of parliament would be transported to Banja Luka, for instance, or to Bileca in Herzegovina, and so on. However, the government operative organs could not get helicopters or anything else. So I spoke about communications from that point of view, and that's how I mentioned being cut off. I mean, not to go into the concept of being cut off from a media point of view - you know, newspapers, journalists. I'm talking about the government. The journalists that were there were mostly in the neighbourhood of the top leadership. It was nicer for them at that altitude rather than up there at the heights where I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric. And I was about to show you a range of communications, military communications in this case, between the 1st Krajina Corps and the Main Staff or the predecessor of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 5th Corps, to the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo from the middle of April to the middle of July --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm afraid you will have to repeat it because I do not get any Serbian translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it any better now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, now I hear it. But the whole question was without translations. I don't know whether witness got it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not. I did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Understood. And I'll repeat that, Mr. Djeric and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was about to show you a range of military communications in this particular instance between the 1st Krajina Corps and the Main Staff, or the predecessor of the 1st Krajina Corps, the 5th Corps, to the 2nd Military District from the period of mid-April 1992 to mid-July 1992. But I take it from your answer that you would not have been privy to those communications and couldn't tell us anything in particular about those.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government did not make use of the military communications system because the prime minister had no relations with the army because the army was under the command of the president of the republic, so the government had nothing to do with it. Secondly, to tell you the truth, I know nothing about military communications. And what you should bear in mind, if it is of any assistance to you, is that until the army left, up until the 20th of May, this whole region in every aspect was under the control of the JNA until it withdrew. After that, the corps of the Army of Republika Srpska inherited it. In other words, the army was a separate mechanism, and they were linked to the Presidency and the president, not the government. And that is the reason why I cannot speak about that, except that I can tell that you we were in isolation, the government was cut off, as a result of the war. The situation was such that due to severed communications, severed roads, et cetera, you couldn't do much. Even if you wanted to do your best, the objective circumstances were such that prevented that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I can -- I'll not present those to the witness, Mr. President. We can bar table those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I did want to ask you about some reflections of the communications that did -- did take place during that period of time through the use of some documents that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could first call up two documents. The first would be P00-- P03922.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document, as you see, sir, dated the 15th April and a decision about the imminent threat of war and the mobilisation of the TO in the whole territory of Serbian BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then if we could turn next 65 ter 17918.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a decision from the ARK region, from the ARK Crisis Staff, referring back to the decision on mobilisation and declaring itself the general public mobilisation on the entire territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. So is it correct, Mr. Djeric, that this would be -- that latter document would reflect the ARK's receipt of and implementation of the mobilisation ordered by the republic authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, in all fairness to the witness, can we just establish the time-frame? I think that the witness should be told that that referred to a period of three weeks, from the 15th of April until the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's down at the bottom of the document. I think that's pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the autonomous region adopted an additional decision on mobilisation. This only confirms how much these local authorities believed in themselves only. And one can confirm that this is a document that they issued on the basis of the document issued by Presidency members, Koljevic and Plavsic, in which they ordered general mobilisation. This goes without saying. Only, one should bear in mind that this still early days. This is the very beginning. But, in spite of that, it was rather belated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that, Mr. President. At least that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] As Exhibit P4985, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, let me turn now to a little bit later in the month, to P02627.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down the page in English, please, and perhaps in B/C/S as well. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Item 9 reflects the reports on the work of crisis staffs, and municipal organs of government were adopted. The reports of Ostojic and, it says, Srbatic - I presume that's Subotic there - are referred to in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could also turn quickly in that connection to 65 ter 09454.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document from Minister Velibor Ostojic reporting on the Serbian TO of the Foca area and their effort to clean up the area and, in the second paragraph, to their liberation of the area of Ustikolina and further information about the situation in liberated areas. Both of those documents, Mr. Djeric, do they also indicate contact and information about the situation in -- and work of the Crisis Staffs and authorities in the various municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with you that that is the case. These are some kind of reports, but I don't know how they reached the council for national security. I cannot confirm anything to that effect. But I can see also that Subotic, who was minister in charge of the military, was also sending reports through some channels of his, whether they be military or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please be fair again. I would like to say that Subotic reported about the conditions prevailing in Sarajevo. That was very close, about 9 kilometres. So it was easy for him to report from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. President, I -- no, let me mention to Mr. Karadzic, I have refrained from commenting at many, many opportunities on the text of documents he's presented. This text is available to everyone, and I'm going to ask that -- the first document was admitted into evidence already - I'm going to ask that document now be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Exhibit P4986, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to turn next to the period of approximately mid-May. That would -- I'm going to skip over, for the moment -- well, that actually moves us past the holding of the 16th Assembly Session in Banja Luka on the 12th of May and all the preparations and communications that would have been necessary to set that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But I'd like to turn to 65 ter 17225. And if we could turn, please, to item 2. That's the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I should mention, first, that this is the minutes of the Sipovo municipal Crisis Staff meeting held on the 15th of May, 1992, as we can see from the first page. Item 2 reflects the request by the Serbian Republic of BH ministry of health and social welfare and to the response of the Crisis Staff to the reading out of that information from the ministry. Mr. Djeric, is this another example of communication between the republic level and a Crisis Staff in the ARK region in the middle of May 1992 -- in this instance, in the middle of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents indicate that the ministry tried to reach the remotest areas and that they were concerned about the situation regarding health and all other necessities, humanitarian and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is what this document shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] As Exhibit P4987, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And two more documents around this particular period of time. The first is P03919.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is a decision on the general public mobilisation of forces and resources in the republic. And the first two items refer to the mobilisation of all military conscripts and the conscripts mentioned in Article 1 and where they are to report, et cetera, and this is dated the 20th of May and signed by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn next to P3537.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is a decision by the Prijedor Crisis Staff at its meeting held on the 22nd of May, 1992, referring to the decision we just looked at, the decision of mobilisation and tracking, as we can see, in the enumerated portions of the document, the order by Mr. Karadzic immediately before that. Mr. Djeric, is this another example of the contact between the republic level and the municipalities and the Crisis Staffs, in this particular instance, an ARK municipality and Crisis Staff, implementing the decision made from the republic level?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This demonstrates that the regional authorities were launching their own initiatives and their government actions based on the decisions from the central government. And you can see that what we discussed yesterday and today, these local factors who were a state within a state, and knowing how the legal system operated, there was no need for the local authorities to declare mobilisation. In addition to that, they didn't have the right to do so. But, as they were a state within a state, all these decisions were adopted in two versions. That is to say, double decisions were adopted. The earlier decision approved -- or issued by the president or Commander-in-Chief, Mr. Karadzic, I suppose that he issued it at the time when he took office, and you can see that before that, two-member Presidency, made up of Koljevic and Plavsic, issued one. And I can only assume that when we had this second wave of mobilisation, we already had Mr. Karadzic as president and that he -- it was he who ordered the mobilisation. So in response to your question, there is synchronicity. There is a certain mode of looking up and copying the acts of the central government which prompted the local government to adopt the decision on the mobilisation. But as I told you, they had no right to do that. That was within the jurisdiction of the central government. So in addition to your question, and I hope I gave you a sufficient answer, you can see here a certain effect of imitation or pretending to be proper authorities. And they were the only authorities in any given area. That was an unavoidable fact. And they didn't bare heed much to what the central government was saying. If they had done that, then they wouldn't hijack any form of authority or cross any boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I'd like to switch topics for a moment and ask you about a couple of the Assembly sessions that Mr. Karadzic spoke to you about yesterday. In particular, he asked you about the 11th Session of the Bosnian-Serb Assembly, which was held on the 18th of March, 1992, and, in particular, quoted some portions about establishing government on the ground, withdrawal from the MUP, and ensuring that everybody felt safe because of the Lisbon Agreement. Now, in connection with the questions Mr. Karadzic asked you about the implementation of the Lisbon Agreement or the Cutileiro Agreement, let me ask you for some additional clarifications, if you can provide them, sir. First of all, is it correct that the Lisbon -- the so-called Lisbon Agreement was not signed and, indeed, the Bosnian Serb leadership emphasised the fact that it had not been signed? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection. Leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm sorry. I can ask that in a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not the Lisbon Agreement had been signed; and do you further recall whether there were references by the Bosnian Serb leadership to whether or not it had been signed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I heard, the Cutileiro Plan was signed. All three sides had agreed and had placed their signatures on the plan. But then later, that's how I know about that, the Muslim side withdrew its signature from the signed agreement. So that's what I know about that. The agreement had been signed and it was effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me turn your attention to a couple of excerpts from that same Assembly session to which Dr. Karadzic drew your attention. The first one is at page -- that's P-- excuse me. That's D00090, and I want to turn your attention to page 6 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I'm afraid that once again this is misleading the witness and creating confusion. It was clearly said that only the maps remained and that that was the reason why it wasn't signed immediately, but the agreement was expressed. And I mentioned during the cross-examination that the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tieger hasn't put his question yet. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I mean, it goes beyond -- I don't want to take time, my time, away from responding to inappropriate commentary. But you're quite right. I'm asking the witness questions, and this is not the opportunity for Mr. Karadzic to put his case or make comments about what deems the evidence to be or not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I'm turning your attention, Mr. Djeric, to two portions of the document. The first is Dr. Karadzic speaking, saying: "The document has been accepted as a basis as a foundation for further negotiations. The document has not been signed. We would never sign anything that we did not agree upon." And then later, at page 42 of the English, which should be either 61 or 62 -- which is 63 -- 62 of the B/C/S, Dr. Karadzic refers to a process and a mistake by a deputy that it was a finished one: "We have entered into this process with our strategic goals and we are accomplishing them stage by stage. We would never have signed this paper as a document. Never, never, never. But at this stage, it would be crazy not to accept it." It goes on at the bottom of the page to point out that they have achieved a certain quality: "And now it will be a question of quantity, and that quantity will happen according to the actual conditions which are up to you to create."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure we are on the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have to scroll down on 42, Mr. President. And it continues on to page 43. That is the actual -- the last portion I quoted is at the topic of page 43 of the English, I believe, and the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, does this refresh your recollection about whether or not the document had been signed; and does it also refresh your recollection about whether or not there was an emphasis by the Bosnian Serb leadership about the fact that it had not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot go any deeper in my answer to this question because I was not involved in those negotiations. And generally speaking, I did not know much about this. So I'm just telling you what was presented to us there, namely that the Lisbon Agreement was practically something that had been concluded. Perhaps there were some minor details that still needed to be done so that the agreement could be implemented. But what was said there, or rather, presented to us, was that historic peace had been achieved, that we could not be dissatisfied, and that we should prepare ourselves for implementing power and justice in the area. This is what I can say about that. But have I never, ever seen any of those agreements. I don't even have an idea where the original documents were kept - any of them - throughout that time. And I know that in the end it would turn out that it's not clear where it is. We don't even know where the original of the Dayton Agreement is, let alone this one. So if you have followed me, I simply can just confirm that we were told, it was presented to us, that the sides had reached an agreement and that it was a historic one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time, so I think it's -- rather than pose the next question, I think it's probably more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much time do you have, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's a little difficult to assess, but I would estimate 15 minutes at this point, but not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take a break for half an hour. 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, in light of your answer just before we adjourned concerning your knowledge of the Cutileiro Agreement, I am not going to take you to some of the excerpts from the 11th Session that. That session is in evidence, and the parties and the Court can review what was addressed during that session at leisure. But I do want to take you to another Assembly session that Mr. Karadzic drew your attention to yesterday, and that's the 17th Assembly Session held on July 24th through 26th, 1992. And that is D00092. And I'd like to begin with a passage that is found at page 14 of the English and page 12 of the B/C/S. And that indicates, in part, some of what had happened between the 11th Session and this 17th Session in July. And that can be found in the middle of the page in English. Actually, toward the bottom -- the -- the last third of the page. This is Dr. Karadzic speaking, and he says: "Today we control all of our territories and perhaps also some territories that will be given to other national communities once a deal is reached." Mr. Djeric, was that -- is that consistent with your recollection of the extent of the territories within Bosnia and Herzegovina that the -- that Bosnian Serb forces controlled by the time of this Assembly session in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question precisely because I'm not sure what the speaker has in mind here when he talks about "control of territory," whether he means the territory controlled by the armed forces. If that's what he means, then he's the only one can know that, because he commanded those troops. So that's what I could say about that. Because the very notion of control, you know, military control is one thing, and control from the point of view of the operational authorities is something else. If you are the ones implementing decisions, organising production, trying to ensure that normal life is functioning, these two things don't have to match. So what is within reach of weapons and whether you believe that territory that you can reach with long-range weapons is territory that is under your control, that's something I cannot really say. Therefore, I cannot say much with precision, whether he means territory in accordance with the Cutileiro Plan or the territory that was the subject of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Would you be able to say whether the territories that Dr. Karadzic is referring to here, including -- included areas where there were large numbers or had been large numbers of non-Serbs living?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see from his statement here. So let me not comment on that. It's clear. He's saying that there are some territories there that would later on be given to the other side in the negotiations. This is how I interpret the thrust of this speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to the territories that were to be retained or that were deemed to be Serbian territory, do you recall references by Dr. Karadzic, or other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, to concerns that the number of Muslims in Republika Srpska represented a potential security threat?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there were such opinions. There were all kinds of people and all kinds of opinions, but that was not the predominant opinion. There are always nationalists and there would always be. There would always be people like Breivik - I'm talking about the incident in Norway - and the like. There were views of that kind. One could hear them. But such views were not predominant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall views that even where the number of Muslims at that moment did not represent an immediate threat that their birth-rate would make them such a security threat in a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people who joined the discussion to express such views. But these are primitive views, views that I do not approve of. I did not approve then, and I do not approve at this moment. You have seen that yesterday I was talking all the time what were the foundations for the legislation and that we insisted on implementing international conventions, international rights, and so on. It was taken into account to preserve everyone's right when such a time came so that the people could enjoy their rights and use them. So that is what was the predominant view. But there were participants in discussion who advocated extremism and the like. That did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me be slightly be more specific with you in that case. Do you recall that Mr. Karadzic expressed such views, including the view that with a sizeable Muslim minority there would be unrest and that that represented a security problem for the state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. Perhaps it was said during some informal conversation or at a deputies' club or some other place where only he was present, but I don't remember that he ever said that in my presence. Even though Mr. Karadzic sometimes allowed himself, being a poet, to make certain excursions which politics do not really bear. So there were all sorts of occasions when he would say various things, and later on I believe he himself realised that some such statements can be interpreted in various ways. But politics, especially when founded on negotiations and agreement, do not allow anything like that. What is necessary is to be clear when advocating certain ideas. And, please, if you allow me, it's very important. I have said earlier, and I state today, that neither myself nor the government were involved in any way in creating policies or defining strategic goals or anything like that. This is easy to check. I was not even aware of those goals, though it would have been natural for the government to prepare certain documents for the Assembly, such as resolutions, declarations, other strategic documents, just like it -- decrees or laws, but the government was never involved in that. The party or the party leadership were the ones doing that, or perhaps Mr. Krajisnik or I don't know who. And then directly, with such formulated views or proposals, they would present them to the Assembly while sidestepping the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned deputies' clubs, for example. I'm not going to take you to references in the deputies' club which this Court has in evidence from 1992. But perhaps I can take you to a reference on this topic in 1995, three years later, which did appear, at least in a -- in the media, in a public form.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would be 65 ter 12703.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to this as being outside of the scope of the direct examination -- or the cross-examination. And to the extent that you find it might be within the scope of the cross-examination, I think this is going to require, out of fairness, a considerable opportunity for Dr. Karadzic to explore this topic. And finally I would ask that you ask Mr. Tieger to conclude in five minutes so that the time-limits that are being applied by the Chamber can be also applied to both sides, since he's already had a considerable time for his re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the Chamber put a time-limit for Mr. Tieger's re-examination, Mr. Tieger -- Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. In fact, you've never put a single time-limit on the Prosecution throughout this entire trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I have to interject. The Prosecution has a very definitive time-limit for its entire case, and they have to work within those parameters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's true Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Judge Morrison. That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, to the Chamber this topic seems to be a new one, given that it's related to 1995 time-frame. So if you like to ask -- put this question, the Chamber will allow the accused to put additional question in relation to this topic. So I'll leave it to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's -- if I can just quickly respond, Mr. President, to that. This did arise out of the cross-examination in respect to leadership objectives or attitudes that was -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we understand that, Mr. Tieger, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- and I'm simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But if you put that question, what I'm saying is that it will allow the accused to put addition questions in relation to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not disputing the Court's ruling, I just want to make sure it's not predicated on the idea that I'm raising a new topic because of the consistencies of views for -- I could have presented the document from 1992 or a number of documents from 1992, but I wanted to show the consistency of view held at that time and -- and remaining until that time, not a new position taken in respect to a new issue. So it's the same issue, is all I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But covering the different time-frame. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think the -- sorry, there seems to be some confusion about the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could try 01339. Then I'd need page 3 of that document. Okay. The original 65 ter I cited, 12073, does have the English linked. That might be a better expedient. In fact it wasn't, and when I originally cited, I transposed the numbers, so it's 12073. And if we could turn to page 3 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S -- sorry, we don't have any B/C/S, and it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And earlier in the article at the top of the page Mr. Karadzic refers to the fact that the Bosnian Serbs are holding more than 70 per cent of the territory. And then if we continue down the page, Dr. Karadzic says: "We don't want more territory as we already have. We don't want to enlarge our state only to have a Muslim minority in it. This would again cause unrest. In five years we would have the next war." Does this refresh your recollection, Mr. Djeric, about whether you heard Mr. Karadzic among those who professed concern about the security risks presented by the number of Muslims who would be within the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to this. Maybe this should be out of the presence of the witness, because I don't want to suggest an answer to him, but I think this is really mischaracterising that text. There's two ways to read that, and certainly one way to read that would be very consistent with what Dr. Karadzic has said along, and has nothing to do with a security risk by a Muslim minority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us ask the witness whether he remembers Mr. Karadzic having said this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But, please, should it be -- should it be presented to the witness literally, what I said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Probably, yes. Did he not read out ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe I did, Mr. President. I can do it again. But I don't see what purpose would be served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, given that we lacked the B/C/S translation, it's important to read it to the witness. Shall we do it again, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I made reference before to the 70 per cent up top. I'm sure I quoted that earlier. Then Mr. Karadzic said -- quote -- he was asked: "Aren't you biting off more than can you chew with regard to your war adventures --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, by the way, are we on the correct page? I'm trying -- I was trying to see the passage, but I couldn't, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's right in front of us; I'll get there in just a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the quote is: "We can roll back those negligible conquests very quickly. But we don't want more territory as we already have. We don't want to enlarge our state only to have a Muslim minority in it. This would again cause unrest. In five years we would have the next war."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Djeric, the -- if you could answer the Court's question which was before you, and that is whether you recall such a statement by Mr. Karadzic. That's the first question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation is not right. It's not the right spirit, and it's also not right in literal terms. Can I please translate this for Mr. Djeric so that he can see verbatim what my answer was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, do you understand English? Do you read English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. [In English] A little. [Interpretation] A bit, a little, but hardly any. Please. When was this stated by Mr. Karadzic -- Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's in May 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, I left in 1992. You heard that. This was in 1995. I do not remember these statements. But this was carried. I don't know whether it's a fact or not. But, in relation to this, I can just say the following. Today, several times, I made statements in relation to certain statements of Mr. Karadzic before the Assembly. So you've been following all of this. You saw the meaning of all of these statements. In these statements, not at any point in time did he bring into question the rights of other ethnic communities, other peoples, to live in Republika Srpska, to enjoy freedom, to use their own property, to exercise their rights, and so on. That is a fact. Those are facts that can be checked, that can be established, and so on. Now, to what extent this statement is correct, I cannot be the judge of that. I can just say that it is an unfortunate circumstance that the war continued. The Cutileiro Plan was an ideal opportunity for peace. It was a good plan. You know that it gave each and every side certain rights, certain territories, and so on. So, as I said, it is unfortunate that peace was not reached in some way. So as war escalated, well, tactics changed. Then approaches to that changed, and so on and so forth. So I cannot -- well, quite simply, I cannot say because I'm not aware of these statements of his. I do not approve of this. I do not support having anyone's rights usurped. You see, I mean, to exercise force in order to bring a people down to a certain percentage, I'm against that. Now, what this statement has to do with the continuation of the war, with its escalation with the intensification of fighting, I mean, I cannot be the judge of that. I mean, these statements of his -- well, I wasn't following that, and I no longer had the opportunity to do so. I don't even know where I was at that point in time, at the point in time when these statements were made. I don't remember. But if -- well, if -- I mean, you know, I do not approve of policies with major territorial ambitions. That would be it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I mean whether Karadzic could and what made him undergo this evolution from the man who made those statements that we looked at to these, well, I cannot say. What kind of political needs were involved, what this was all about. I mean, since I disagreed with many things - I've already said that - I did not take part in defining the objectives, and so on and so forth. Whether this had to do with the political party as such, only Mr. Karadzic can say. I do not approve of any policies that have at their forefront the territorial --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, you see where this leads to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's not for you to intervene at this time. Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to tender that and conclude my re-direct examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are tending this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I don't see any basis to admit this through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I can do so with the bar table. I'm happy to do it that way. I understand the rules that have applied to admission through witnesses. I would say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So how can you guarantee that Mr. Karadzic said this actually to -- to the journalist?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can't guarantee it in the sense the Court is asking me that, but that is a matter that goes to weight in light of all the totality of the evidence and other statements that Mr. Karadzic made to the same effect or to contrary effects, and the Court weighs that in the mix.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And you concluded your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'd like to call your attention to one issue that's been floating around in written materials this week, and that relates to the bar table motions of the Prosecutor and our position that intercepted conversations have to be put to a witness when the witness has been called by the Prosecution. There are five intercepted conversations in the Prosecution's bar table motion, second bar table motion, in which Prime Minister Djeric is one of the participants. And, for example, in 65 ter 30688 on the 20th of April, 1992, they want to admit an intercepted conversation between Prime Minister Djeric and Momcilo Mandic, in which they discuss barricades being put up in Ilidza. And the Prosecution contends that the probative value of this is to show that the leadership, Prime Minister Djeric presumably and Dr. Karadzic, was exercising control over the barricades. That's a very controversial issue and certainly one I would imagine Prime Minister Djeric might not agree with. And so this illustrates our point that it's unfair to admit from the bar table intercepts of witnesses who are here to testify. So I would ask that you ask the Prosecution either to put those intercepts to this witness or to withdraw them from their bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why did Mr. Karadzic not put such a question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Two reasons. Number one, we don't know whether they'll be admitted or whether they're part of the Prosecution case until you rule it on the bar table motion. And secondly, you didn't give him enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, you're also referring to the inefficiency of time for his cross-examination even after having observed how he spent his -- most of time. Let's leave it at that. But, yes, Mr. Tieger, do you have any observation as to the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, a couple, Mr. President. First of all, this issue was raised and ruled on before. We make that point in our response to the bar table submission commentary, as -- if I recall correctly. It this would be in -- this is another occasion when the Defence is ignoring the Court's previous rulings and seeking to reverse a previous practice. And furthermore, it's very clear that, in a case of this magnitude, matters -- not -- and I think the Court made this point previously - this issue can only go to the weight, and we -- both parties accept that some issues are more fulsomely thrashed out and therefore the Court is in a position to allocate a greater amount of weight to that particular piece of information based on the courtroom colloquies. Other pieces of information the Court has weight based on the totality of the evidence, and that's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, my question is: Irrespective of the debate as to the bar table motion, to put it short - let's put it short - whatever the ruling may be, that you are not minded to put questions to Mr. Djeric about the intercept where he is one of the interlocutors?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I misunderstood the Court's question. That's correct, Mr. President. I'm not. And we rely on the Court's previous ruling and on the strength of our position in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Unless other members of the Bench have questions for you, that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just put three brief questions and the Professor can give just a yes or no answer?
