utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. Then it concludes your evidence, Mr. Djeric. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I felt it was my moral obligation. That's why I came. I thank you very much. And may justice prevail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would like to join in this gratitude and also to wish the witness a safe journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the fact that the next witness is a protected witness and we need at least five minutes to set up the courtroom accordingly, we'll rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.35 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a few questions, but first I want to show you a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 90331, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've been granted protective measures in this case, which means we won't be using your name or any other information that could identify you, so you have to be careful as well not to do that. My question now: The piece of paper you see before you, if you could please just "yes" or "no," do you see your name written on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I tender that under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4988, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I have just a couple of questions for you now about testimony you gave in a previous case. You remember that you testified in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could you please confirm to Their Honours two things: that you've reviewed that testimony and it's accurate; and that if I was to ask you the same questions today as in that case, your answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would admit that, then, as the 92 ter statement. It's 65 ter 22756A and should be under seal, and the same number ending in B is a public redacted version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both of them will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4989 under seal and Exhibit P4990, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be best at this time to tender the one and only associated exhibit which I'm moving -- which I seek to tender, and that's 03453, the pseudonym sheet from the prior case. 03453.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That would be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4991, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now read a brief summary of the statement. Shortly after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995, the witness was present on an occasion at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. A VRS officer there introduced himself as Colonel Beara. Colonel Beara stated that they had a lot of prisoners held at various locations in the municipality and it was hard to control them. Beara said that they had to get rid of the prisoners and that they would need assistance in burying the bodies. Colonel Beara said that the order to get rid of the prisoners had come from two presidents. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much. I don't have any questions for you now. So I'm finished for now. I may have some questions later. But Mr. Karadzic will have some questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Witness, as you noted, your evidence which was given in the Popovic et al. case was admitted in its entirety in lieu of your oral testimony in this case in your evidence in-chief. Now you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one thing. As Mr. Nicholls explained it to you, that you are being protected with pseudonym and image and voice distortion, in the course of your answering the question, whenever you feel that your answer might reveal your identity, please don't hesitate to tell us to go into private session, which will not broadcast outside. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Witness, I would like to express my gratitude to you for having been in contact with the Defence, albeit via videolink, just like with the OTP. Nevertheless, I would like to remind you, as I'm reminding myself, that we should pause between questions and answers because the interpreters cannot keep up. I would like to ask you to be mindful of the transcript. The moment the typing stops, the interpretation is over, in most cases. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would immediately like to move on to the Prosecutor's summary. Can you confirm that this was on the 15th? Or what was the date? This encounter that is described in the summary.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date because I was contacted by the OTP 11 years after those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you were not asked personally to attend but that it was someone who was asking to see someone from the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Since I do not remember that there was a direct telephone call made to me, rather, it was the secretary who conveyed to me that I'm being asked to speak to someone from the brigade, I inferred that they were looking for someone from the municipality, so I went to the brigade, not knowing who it was that was asking to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that that was not a formal meeting; rather, it was just people standing and talking briefly?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes. Also I said in my statement that there was no procedural meeting. Rather, at the entrance to one of the offices of Zvornik Brigade, there was this gentleman, and he stood there with his security people, and I stood there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that this was communicated to you as something that your consent was not required for? You were just asked to render a service, if you will.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you were shocked and that you did not dare put too many questions, except for a question by way of a phrase, and then this colonel answered that that had been ordered by two presidents or communicated by two presidents?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: There was no dialogue at the municipality. It was only the colonel who spoke. I did not ask anything; whereas he, in this same tone, uttered that sentence. It was a monologue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he explain or could one know or could one conclude unequivocally which presidents he was preferring to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: I did not ask, and I did not understand either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Knowing me, and as for the extent to which you knew me and other things - we will discuss that later - did you think it was plausible that I would order or approve of executions of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Knowing you, after having seen you for more than 20-odd times at various meetings, I did not believe for a moment that you could order any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We met after that event as well a few times. These were official meetings or others that were more casual. Was it your conclusion that I knew anything about that? Was that being discussed at all? Did anyone talk about that? Did anyone inform you about that during these encounters of ours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer -- Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, but I would request that that question be broken up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we meet, after this occasion, on several other occasions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes, we did meet several times. And they were different topics that were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On those occasions, did anyone talk about this? Did anyone inform me? Was there any mention of this incident, or this actual event, that had to do with the meeting with this colonel?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: That topic was not broached ever, nor was it ever mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you draw your conclusions about whether I knew anything about this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: From your conversations and the problems that we dealt with, one could not infer that you knew anything about it. And you never asked us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Even when I was not present, was this a taboo, something that not many people wanted to broach or talk about, this incident? Not -- so I'm not referring just to the meeting, but also everything that may have happened in that area after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: That topic was, like, prohibited. But, in fact, no one ever mentioned it, except in very unusual circumstances. There may have been one or two persons who mentioned this or talked about this, but -- and they would talk about it privately, but it was never discussed in a broader meeting, where more people were present, nor was this incident analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the interview, you accepted and you understood that the colonel in question perhaps, when he mentioned the two presidents, was trying to impress those present and, thus, ensure that his request is implemented. Would you allow for such a possibility, as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like a cite, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take that to mean that his -- his interview via videolink that he had with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, if that's the case, I'm sorry, I thought he meant the OTP interview.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You're right, Excellency, yeah. [Interpretation] That's correct, that's from the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And in the course of this interview with Mr. Karadzic, I did say that it was possible that the monologue and the tone of this person probably could suggest that he was trying to impress upon the others that this was something that was a binding order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now is it correct that he explained, or, rather, referred to the danger of holding such a large number of prisoners if someone from the column was -- would launch an attack or if an attack would be launched from Kalesija from the other side? Did he mention this threat, this danger? When he talking about having to get rid of them, did he mention what his reasons were and what his fears were and why it was that this -- that he would have to get rid of them and what those fears might be?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: He said that he could not control them, that he had to get rid of them. Now, whether he knew anything about the column that was moving towards Zvornik and that was concentrating on the other side, towards Tuzla, and that we from the Zvornik municipality sent an appeal to the court to be -- to be allowed to have our brigade returned to Zvornik because of this threat, I cannot really draw any conclusions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You cannot conclude that he knew what you knew; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes. In Zvornik, we knew what the threat was. We knew how endangered we were, because all the mobilised soldiers were outside of Zvornik municipality territory. And there was a group of over -- several thousand Muslims moving from Srebrenica through Zvornik municipality, and we did not know whether they were headed for Zvornik or, as it turned out, to Federation territory, which is where they later went, passing through the municipality. (redacted) (redacted) asked that our brigade, which at that point in time was in Zepa municipality, be sent back, or at least parts of the brigade, so that they could protect our town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, when the colonel talked about not being able to control them, did he use any epithets saying these are beasts or anything to that effect? Did you know a man who drove them and who witnessed, who actually saw weapons being grabbed by these men and shooting and so on? So without mentioning the name of this person, could you tell us whether he talked about how he couldn't control these people, that they were beasts, and did you somehow link that with what you knew?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: The colonel said in this very short monologue - and I have to stress that - he said that he could not control them, that they were dangerous, and the rest, what I've already mentioned. And as for the events that I had learned from some other sources, that came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You learned about that later on; correct? If it would make you feel better, perhaps we could move briefly to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope I will be done before the break. I don't want to keep you here very long. But I would like now to briefly discuss several topics with you before -- things before this incident, but let's just finish with the incident. You yourself did not have -- were not involved in any way in this, and you don't know whether anyone actually acted on the demand by this colonel; or do you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: I had no further involvement in this, and I was not in Zvornik municipality at all, and I don't know -- I don't know how this all ended or who actually acted on those orders or demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to go briefly to 1994, and I will --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And please try to answer my questions with a yes or a no so that we can complete before the break. Now, is it correct that life before the first multi-party elections was rather normal, more or less, until the SDA decided to secede from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you were present and you were even close to me during one of -- during a convention in the summer of 1992 in a room full of people where Mr. Adil Zulfikarpasic and I addressed the audience, that was a mixed audience, and tried to describe the meaning of the historic Serb -- Serbian/Muslim agreement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that meeting. It was in a sports hall in Zvornik. I was one of the people who provided security there, although the meeting was peaceful, and we considered that that was a historic attempt at reconciliation, or, rather, survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of Yugoslavia. And the audience, the people who were there, were delighted that we managed to meet, that we managed to have a common position with the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when this agreement was rejected by the SDA and where it was agreed that the municipality of Zvornik should now be divided into two municipalities, where one would be predominantly Serb and one predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: After the conclusion of the local elections, the authorities were set up in Zvornik, and they were divided between the Serbs and the Muslims. All the officials were left in their posts, and the politicians from the party were conducting negotiations about a peaceful resolution of any problems, and they were doing that round the clock. They also negotiated about the division of the Zvornik municipality into a Serbian and a Muslim part. I can tell you that the borders for the division were something that we always had diametrically opposed views about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the SDA undermined the negotiations and that in the meantime it had set up the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, that is to say, two paramilitary formations, in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: The position of the representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party was that the municipality should be divided geographically and that the town of Zvornik should be divided as well. The northern part was to belong to the Serbs and the southern part to the Muslims. On the other hand, the SDA representatives requested that the separation line should be drawn in such a way that even the smallest place populated by the Bosniaks should belong to the Muslim side, and that was where we had completely opposed -- opposed views. And as for weapons, we had information, there were rumours going around, that they were arming themselves through the interior ministry and that they had those paramilitary formations, that is to say, the Green Berets and the Patriotic League who were stationed somewhere up on Godus, that they were having training, and we received this information from our activists from border villages Rastosnica and Boskovici. Therefore, the situation was tense and it was always on the verge of an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move into private session for just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I was somewhat an optimist in my assessment. I would need another 15 minutes or so after the break, but I would certainly spend less time than I have been allotted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you -- you think it would be convenient to break now? Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so. I should not embark on another topic if I'm unable to conclude it before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will have a break for an hour and resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Morrison will not attend the remainder of today's session and first part of tomorrow's session due to an official business. We'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were talking about JNA units and the unit which had come close to Zvornik. Judging by your experience, did the JNA at the time had an equally unfriendly attitude to the SDA and other parties? Because you said in your interview they didn't like us a lot or they didn't have a high opinion of us, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: The JNA was insisting on multi-ethnicity at the time. However, those who responded to mobilisation call-ups were mostly the Serbs, and I have to note that there (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: (redacted) And as is well known, the JNA was indoctrinated by communism and it did not have a high opinion of nationally oriented political parties, including the SDS among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me first finish with this topic. Is it true, however, that very soon after that the JNA realised that it felt safe only in Serb-populated areas?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Well, essentially, no one responded to mobilisation call-ups from among the Bosniaks, and probably they felt safer in Serbian territory because the composition of their units was such that the troops were mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this because I wonder if you agree and if you knew that on the 5th of April in Sapna a JNA column was passing through on its way to Yugoslavia for which it was leaving [as interpreted]. An attack was launched on it, and a young second lieutenant was killed and other people were wounded. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It was a big incident at the time. As the JNA officers used to move freely around all of the Bosnia-Herzegovina territory, it was a great surprise for us that someone had killed an officer. That caused a huge revolt on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did the units that you were familiar with also see that as a heavy blow?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: It was one of the major events during that period. And my recollection is that after that incident many able-bodied Serbs came to our unit asking to be issued uniforms and weapons, and they wanted to place themselves voluntarily at the disposal of the JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was nobody else that they could report themselves to at that moment? I mean on the 5th of April. In other words, that there were no Serbian paramilitaries originating from the Serbs, or manned by the Serbs, that they could have reported themselves to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: The Serbian people placed great trust in the Yugoslav People's Army. At that moment, there were no Territorial Defence units organised by places, and it was only a normal reaction of the population that it requested protection and also weapons from the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I conclude my questioning, I would like to ask you the following: Am I right if I say that had Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic's idea of a historic agreement between the Serbs and the Muslims had prevailed, is it true that Bosnia, as a single state in your municipality, as a single unified entity, had remained in Yugoslavia, that no one would have moved anywhere? Was that what the concept envisaged, a peaceful resolution and continuation of co-existence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: The only condition imposed by the Serbian people, and our policy at the time, was that Bosnia-Herzegovina remain integrated in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: And Zulfikarpasic's concept at the moment only confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right about this: When we saw that they wanted to secede and when the talks about transforming the municipality into two separate municipalities began, am I right when I say that not even in that case no one would have moved out of Zvornik unless the Muslims would have moved from the Serbian part of town to the Muslim municipality but without being persecuted? Was the idea to provide security to everyone so that everyone would enjoy the rights in their own municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Well, I'm convinced there would have been no interethnic conflict at all if Bosnia had remained integrated in Yugoslavia and if the referendum on cessation had not been held, which the international community recognised, by the way, though it did not recognise the decision of the Serbian people to remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could you tell me whether this concept of having two municipalities implied some sort of expulsion of movement of population, or would the entire population have remained in the territory of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: This concept of two municipalities implied that a division of Bosnia should be -- should be avoided and that, therefore, the conflict would be avoided also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of additional questions, though you were not in the town itself, or maybe you were later on. Did you learn anything about the events up until the 8th of April and after that. Or, to be more precise, after this murder of an officer that I mentioned, did the Muslim paramilitary formations control Zvornik, whereas the Serbian population had left across the river to Serbia, so that men slept in Serbia during the night and returned to Zvornik to work, whereas the women and children remained in Zvornik or perhaps up in Karakaj and other Serb-populated parts of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: We were located in Celopek, five kilometres away from Zvornik, and it was not a good idea to go to the town of Zvornik wearing our JNA uniforms. We were warned against that. It was well-known that as the bridge across the Drina was there, the Serbian men went to Serbia for the night and then, in the morning, would return to Zvornik to work, over these several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you witness that the first refugees after the outbreak of the conflict were Serbs from Central Bosnia and that in Zvornik, at the beginning, they were accommodated in the sports hall, and in villages they would sometimes turn up as well, and they would enter Muslim homes not really in a violent manner but not very peacefully either? Can you say something to the Trial Chamber about the arrival of refugees to the town, their accommodation in the sports hall, and the turning up of refugees in Muslim-populated villages?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: In Zvornik we had a great influx of refugees from Tuzla and Kladanj. On one particular day, several thousand refugees arrived and were accommodated in the sports hall. They left of their own free will in an organised manner, though, they would go to surrounding villages populated by Muslims, and under pressure they would move into their houses; whereas, they would leave, taking with them what they could carry in their hands, and they would go in the direction of the Federation or -- otherwise they would cross over to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the local authorities were not involved in that at all and that very often they would learn only later on what had happened?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: The local authorities, in the first days and during the first month, did not have practically any power because the paramilitaries were rampant at the time, and there was a general situation of lawlessness so that no one could have co-ordinated the reception of refugees and their accommodation. Everything was out of control and out of hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You now meant the Serbian paramilitaries. Could you please enumerate several of those groups and tell the Trial Chamber who held the power in Zvornik at the time. Is it correct that your unit was threatened, that they threatened some soldiers that they would be shot by a firing squad? And give us a picture of this situation of lawless in Zvornik at the time.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Just like in any system where there is no discipline and no authority, the weapons were those that ruled. During the first days, the Arkan volunteers who liberated Zvornik imposed themselves as the ones who held power. Other volunteers were arriving on a daily basis. They joined the JNA units. There were also individual paramilitary units from the Croatian front. They had experience and they knew how to intimidate the population. They had all kinds of names. They glorified their own power, and they spread fear among the population. They would even strip people naked, I mean the Serbs, and then chase them through villages naked, to serve as an example if they failed to respond to call-ups for mobilisation and were disobedient. There were also several incidents of people who were beaten up, and grown-up people were forced to go naked through Celopek so that they would be seen by their relatives and everyone else who happened to be present. So the overall security level was very low, and if you believe me, even I, though I had some experience - I had been in the army for six month - I was not brave enough to go to Zvornik, especially not in the evening, or to drive my own car, because it would have been hijacked or stolen. Nobody was feeling safe at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that many of them came regularly as volunteers, which was approved by decrees and by law, and very soon many of them would become outlaws; they would refuse to remain on the lines but they would rather return to the town to do all of these things that you have just described for us?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: The paramilitary formations were stationed in the town. During day-time, they would go into the field to defend the territory and help the population, allegedly. However, in the evening they were always quartered in the town, and there they had the power that no one could challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there any force, any armed force, such as the military or police in Zvornik that could resolve the problem, have them arrested or expel them? I mean any local force.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: No. At the beginning, no local force could have resolved the issue about these paramilitaries, nor did anyone try. Only later on when the Army of Republika Srpska was established, then some sort of an order was established, even though they also had some units which did not want to place themselves under army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that a large-scale operation was planned and then carried out by the special police brigade from Pale with the assistance of police from Serbia and the assistance of the protection regiment, the 65th Protection Regiment, and that approximately at the end of July these units were arrested, liquidated, or expelled?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. It was all of a sudden that the special police units from Pale had arrived. I don't know who else. And that under the leadership of Officer Karisik, they rounded up and arrested those so-called Yellow Wasps. That is to say, one of the most notorious units in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I usually don't do that, but I wish to offer you to say something if I -- if there's something that you consider significant and that I did not ask you about, something that would be important for my case.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. I believe that you should be held responsible if you are guilty and that you should be freed if you are innocent. It is up to the Court to determine that. I wish you a lot of luck.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: (redacted) How did you see me?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Well, probably it can be noticed from my testimony, I cannot even imagine that you were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked about Arkan in a little bit on the cross-examination. Would you characterise him as a paramilitary leader?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Sometimes yes; sometimes no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay. When yes; when no?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: No in terms of system of warfare and discipline; and yes on the basis of what was done after an operation would be over. Later, they were prone to looting just like all other paramilitaries, whereas in action they were highly disciplined and they obeyed their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think I understand, but just let me make sure. So in April of 1992, when Arkan's Men, as you say, liberated Zvornik, in the military aspect they were professional, but then these troops committed crimes, looting, ethnic cleansing, things like that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this ethnic cleansing cannot be accepted unless an objection is raised. Because this implies putting words into the witness's mouth. It's not even leading. It is simply putting words into the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you reformulate the question, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Yeah, I'll re-form the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you understood what I was saying was, if I understood you, during the combat operations to liberate Zvornik you regarded Arkan's Men as good soldiers but afterwards they committed crimes. Is that -- did I understand you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: No. I didn't talk about crimes. Like other paramilitaries, they were prone to looting property and to robbery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But aren't those crimes?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: A type of crime. Probably. But I'm not a lawyer, and I cannot be sure about that. If somebody steals something and drives it away, it's probably a crime, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yeah. Do you know who Dragan Spasojevic is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what was his position in April 1992 in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And while he was police commander, did he have anything to do with Arkan's Men coming to Zvornik? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: On several occasions, he himself said that that was his merit. That is to say, that he brought Arkan to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And after they had been in Zvornik, after the liberation of Zvornik, was it clear to you and others that this paramilitary group was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Has the microphone been activated? Mr. Karadzic, are you receiving translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After the liberation of Zvornik, and I'm just trying to get the time in context, was it clear to you then, and others, that Arkan's Men were responsible for looting, robbery - these other acts you talked about?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: At that moment, for us they were heros. We had great fear of the Muslim army and the Muslim population because our numbers were smaller, and we never had the courage to go out and liberate Zvornik as units of the local population of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And I'm asking about afterwards. You talked about how once these groups stayed, that they committed looting and robbery. Was Arkan's group one of those? We've already talked about this.

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: Yes. They took trucks, trailer trucks that were socially owned. Also cars, et cetera. However, we didn't consider that to be a loss. It was more important for us to have freedom and to be safe, safe from enemy attacks, and to know that we could defend ourselves. At such moments, the struggle for life, survival, is more important than the material. Whoever is helping you survive is more important to you than anyone else. It is hard to explain this to people who had never participated in this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene. The witness did not say it is hard to explain to someone who did not participate. The witness said it is hard for someone who never participated in this kind of thing to understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And are you also aware whether Arkan's Men committed crimes against the Muslim population during the liberation? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: I'm receiving no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: I can hear you throughout, but I don't have any interpretation. I do not hear the B/C/S interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Our usher will help you, will check the headphone first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a while, I wasn't receiving any either, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you now hear me in the language you understand, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. So why don't you repeat the previous question of yours, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just very quickly. My question that you didn't get was: Are you also aware whether Arkan's Men committed crimes against the Muslim population during the liberation of Zvornik? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: During the liberation of Zvornik, I, together with my unit, was at a feature on the right-hand side on a hill from which you could see Zvornik. I did not take part in the liberation of Zvornik directly during those few hours, and I did not see them commit crimes, kill the innocent population. So, as for these events, I am not a person who can provide the right information for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you hear about them committing crimes against the Muslim population either in Zvornik or Bijeljina, where they were just before; did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: It is hard to give an answer to that question because in that period, as one reads the newspapers and follows trials, it is hard. All sorts of things have been written. And also during certain previous trials arguments and counter-arguments were presented in terms of their action in Bijeljina and Zvornik, so I really cannot give you an answer that would satisfy you. I can just say that they were heros among the population because they helped them overcome their fear and they helped them feel safe. Now, whether they committed crimes, I only know about stories that someone had been killed somewhere, but it's not that I spoke to eye-witnesses myself. Therefore, I cannot give you an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so let me see if I understand you correctly. Is Arkan a hero to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness said the population. He did not speak of himself. This is a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [Overlapping speakers] ... there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. No need. It's not for you to intervene at this stage, Mr. Karadzic. Could you answer the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that at that moment, during these operations, people were afraid, and that he, Arkan, was a hero among the population. I was in a unit that was in the service of its people. If Arkan committed crimes, he's not a hero, and -- now, now, it's not with 100 per cent certainty that I can say that Arkan personally took part in the liberation of Zvornik. It was Major Pejic that led his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, his deputy. Now, there's evidence in this trial that the VRS had to expel Arkan's Men from Zvornik, force them out. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: I did not quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was Arkan's Men one of the paramilitaries that had to be forcibly removed from Zvornik to restore order by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: No. They left after four or five days. On their own. On their own. And they created such chaos. They withdrew all the Serb forces from Zvornik, and -- I mean, to the Alhos base in Karakaj, and then they got into their vehicles and went to Serbia. At that moment, Zvornik was empty. It was an empty town without a single soldier to defend it, and the civilian population had not returned yet. So Arkan's Men were there for a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you talked about Mr. Karadzic and your knowledge of him. Do you know that he invited Arkan's troops back into the RS in 1995? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Prosecutor provide a reference? Where was it that I invited Arkan? And which document confirms that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yeah, it's very clear from Mr. Milovanovic's testimony. I don't have the cite at the moment. General Milovanovic, I should say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Milovanovic corrected himself here. He said: Until recently, I believe that you had asked him to come, and just recently, I've learned the truth. So it was incorrectly cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you: Do you know whether Mr. Karadzic invited Arkan's Men to the RS in 1995?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: I did not hold any kind of high office at state level to know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so you don't know about his relationship with Arkan or other paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you seen the video in September 1995 of Arkan saluting President Karadzic in Bijeljina before he goes back to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ320
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, during the course of your testimony, you stated that you knew the driver who carried the prisoner [sic] to the Kravica warehouse and witnessed the killing. Could you repeat what you heard from that driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The driver was driving prisoners. This bus was full, and the security was provided by one or two policemen with automatic rifles. At one point in time, the prisoners grabbed the policemen's rifles and started shooting. The police that were outside, or the military units that were outside, then started firing at the bus. Then they took everyone out of the bus, the driver included, and someone recognised the driver and took him away from the other prisoners; whereas, all the prisoners from that bus were executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to him, what did he do afterwards? Did he drive the bus back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only ten days later did he manage to get the bus working again. He did not take part in the transportation because his bus had broken down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to him, how long did they stay there in front of Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't come home for three or four days. He slept there as well. He spent a few days there. Now, was it in Kravica or on the bus or with a local person, I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he say that he also witnessed the killing of people who were inside the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He only talked about his bus and that one incident with the people who were on board the bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, do you have the 65 ter number of this witness's first interview where he talked about this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I do, Your Honour. It's 03459, and it's pages 24 to 25, really 23 to 25, of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank you and applaud you for being conscientious so that that testimony could be heard in public session. We appreciate that very much. There was one other aspect that was mentioned in private session that I think should also be part of the public record, which deals with the fact that he testified that there were prisoners who had grabbed the rifles from the guards and that -- then after that, the guards began shooting. So I wonder if we could simply ask the witness to confirm that while we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, you heard what Mr. Robinson, who is the legal advisor for Mr. Karadzic, said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He said that just now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 80, line 8, on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I think that's evident. Or just in case ... You heard Mr. Robinson's words. Can you confirm that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The incident occurred when the prisoners snatched away the weapons from the policemen and shot. The reaction was that the others shot at the bus. And later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Witness. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but please wait for the moment so that arrangements can be made. We'll draw the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is available. It just will take us a couple of minutes to re-sort our materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break for five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 2.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Tabeau. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Yes. Would you introduce your expert, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. It is with pleasure that I wish to introduce to you Dr. Stevo Pasalic, who is a Defence expert for demographic issues and issues of demographic losses during the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Pasalic. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I also introduce Mr. Jason File who is a new lawyer to the Karadzic team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome, Mr. File. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ah, good afternoon. Ma'am, as the Trial Chamber knows, you used to work here at the OTP. But can you tell us where you work now?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I work in a research --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not sure ... yes, it's there, now activated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I am now working in a research institute. The name of this institute is Agricultural Economics Institute, part of the University of Wageningen. I am having there -- I started there in September last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is the subject matter of your work there?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I am involved in two projects. One of these projects is related to the study of food security, global food security. The second project in which I'm involved is a project related to bio-based economy.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And may we have 65 ter 04103, please. 65 ter 04103.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, we understand that you worked for OTP from 2000 to 2011. What was your role?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I was the head of the demographic unit, the Office of the Prosecutor, and I also was doing a lot of research related to victims of the wars, 1990s wars, in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I understand that your doctorate is mathematical demography. Is that the subject matter of the subject study that you applied to your work at OTP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I have education that is relevant for the type of work I was doing at the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And prior to 2000, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I worked here in the Netherlands in -- in another research institute, in the National Demographic Institute of the Netherlands. I spent there nine years, from 1991 to August, I think, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Now, yes. Yes, I was waiting for the translation to be completed. Now you can put the next question, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: While you were at that institute, tell us what type of work you did.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I was doing scientific research related to mortality and causes of death. I was involved in projects on modelling of mortality in Western Europe, including the Netherlands, other Western European countries. I also studied mortality and causes of mortality in countries of Central and Eastern Europe. I worked on prospects for life expectancy and longevity.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, from May to September in 2009, did you work for the Cambodian Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. I had a project of five months in 2009 in which I completed a report, expert report, on victims of the Khmer Rouge regime in Cambodia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on the screen in front of us we see your CV, and we don't see the second page, but can you tell us whether your CV highlights a number of your publications.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. There is a small number of selected publications. It is not the complete list of all papers I have published. It is just the most recent and most relevant probably as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Have you testified here before as an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. I testified in total 17 times in various cases, including the highest profile cases, like Slobodan Milosevic, Vojislav Seselj, Krajisnik, sorry, not in Krajisnik, actually. In Sarajevo cases, General Galic and Dragomir Milosevic and, of course, in Srebrenica cases, in Tolimir and Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we tender 65 ter 04013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, for this case there are three components upon which you wrote reports, and the first component we're going to talk about is the municipality component. And can you tell the Court generally what your task was in that regard?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, to make clear what is the municipality component, I would like to refer to the report, expert report I made on this subject. It is --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For the record, that is 65 ter 10723.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The title of this report is: Ethnic Composition and Displaced Persons and Refugees in 27 Municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1991 and 1997. This is a report that summarizes changes in the ethnic composition and population movements, external and internal, all related to the war from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I'd like now to talk about the sources that you would use in order to come to conclusions. But first, can you give us a general idea of what demographers would normally used in order to come to figures regarding population shifts?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I think the best source that could be used in this type of work is the population census. I would most certainly select two censuses, the one before the conflict and the other one after the conflict, and I would compare information from the censuses in order to draw conclusions related to ethnic composition and displacement. I would also look for migration sources. That would be registers of population movements. Migration registers are very frequent, as the population movements are usually extremely dynamic, especially in conflict situation. It is hard to record this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as regards the reports that you wrote for this case, were those types of sources available?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, partly yes. On one hand, we used the population census for Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1991, March 1991, which is a census that describes the population at the outbreak of the conflict. And because there was no next census, and still at this moment the next census for Bosnia has not been conducted, we looked for sources that could be used as a reliable replacement. And this reliable replacement of post-conflict census were the voters registers from 1997 municipal elections and 1998 parliamentary and presidential elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 11218, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, while we wait for that to come up, as part of your report you included an annex to a previous report that you had written, and we're looking at that annex right now. The annex to the Milosevic report. Do you refer to this annex in your Karadzic report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. The report we are discussing right now is the so-called addendum to the Slobodan Milosevic report that was produced in 2003. So the word "addendum" is used, only means that it is -- what we present for the Karadzic case is based on the same sources, the same methodology as were used for the Slobodan Milosevic report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what we see in front of us, Annex B, overview of sources, is this something that is applicable to the Karadzic municipality report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is a relevant annex where sources are discussed. I didn't mention one important source. In addition to the 1991 census and voters registers, I also used the records of displaced -- internally displaced persons and refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina that were compiled with involvement of the UNHCR and the government in the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to talk about these sources in detail. And the first one I'd like to talk about is the census. When was the census taken?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The census that -- the 1991 census was taken physically from 1st to the 15th of April, 1991, and reported on the status of -- in the families of those interviewed as of 31st of March this year, of course, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did the census cover the entire population of the country?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Census is the most complete source, large survey, covering the entire population.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how were the interviews conducted?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: The interviews were conducted in person with heads of households in all households in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were trained interviewers who were completing the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were those interviews face to face?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- these were face-to-face interviews based on a standardised questionnaire developed by professional statisticians.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us what information was collected from each person.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it was a census that was describing the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also housing conditions and agricultural farms. So there were, like, three groups of questions that were asked for this work -- on this case and other cases. The part related to persons was most essential. Names were collected; date of birth; personal identification number, called JMBG; ethnicity; religion; marital status; children ever born; education; type of job; professional level, et cetera, et cetera. A very extensive record of the information about persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is this a typical type of information that would be asked in a census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. This is a standardised questionnaire that conforms to general rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You mentioned a personal identification number called the JMBG. Was this a unique number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, this is a unique number. It started to be issued in the -- in 1980, around 1980, in the former Yugoslavia. Normally children, newborn children, were assigned this number at birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What significance did this number have in your research?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It has a lot of significance because it is unique and because it is also reported in my post-war sources on the population, the voters registers. And having such a unique number associated with each person in both sources that I studied made it possible for me to draw the conclusions described in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I think you also mentioned that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Given the technical nature, interpreters need more time in particular in case of French and B/C/S translation. So if you could pause between the question and answers, please. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I thought I heard you mention ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Ethnicity was reported in the census.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please tell us what the process was for reporting ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In the questionnaire used in the 1991 census, ethnicity was described by an open-ended question. That means there were no predefined categories included for the interviewed person to select one from a list. Persons could report any ethnicity they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, now, for persons who were interviewed who were employed persons, persons who had jobs, what was the source of data regarding their JMBG, or the personal identification number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: For the employed persons, in addition to the questionnaire that was filled with the interviewer, another portion of information was collected during the census from their employers. So employers provided information about various aspects of the employee, including the JMBG number, the unique number, based on which many analyses were completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us how the authorities processed the census information.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is a huge survey, the population census. The population size of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991 was approximately 4.4 million individuals. This number of questionnaires to put on record electronically was -- was -- electronically scanned. Optical scanning methods were applied to get the data from the questionnaires in the computer files. Of course, before the scanning could started -- could start, there was a process of preparing the questionnaires for the scanning. Special codes were used to code reported answers on the questionnaires, and these codes were later included in the computer files. Optical scanning was the method of entering data.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And ultimately was a quality control imposed on the data?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Of course. Quality control started already in municipalities. There were municipality commissions that were responsible for the correctness of completing the census, so they were the first one to complete -- to correct -- to check the completeness and correctness of taking the census. They counted the questionnaires. So a lot of work was already done there. Later they were continued in the central statistical office in Sarajevo, who was able to finish the checks for the population part of the census. They didn't finish checks of the agricultural census and households.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So was there only one portion of the census --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may correct. It is not "households" I wanted to say. Houses, housing. The apartments part of the census. It is not households.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So my question is: Was the population part of the census completely finished before the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now I want to talk to you about the second source you mentioned, voters registers. Are you familiar with the organisation OSCE?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. It is Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. It is an organisation that is mandated to monitor and assist in -- in the conduct of elections, especially in countries, post-conflict countries like Bosnia-Herzegovina, OSCE played an important role to ensure that elections were conducted in a proper way. And they were -- there was no fraud.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you write about this particular source in Annex B as well?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. That is a description of the voters register from 1997/1998 and, of course, the role of OSCE in running these elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, tell us the circumstances upon which OSCE was in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It was just after the conflict ended, and the situation in the country was still unstable. There were political tensions and social tensions. Economically there were problems. So in these kind of situations it is important that no side would be using elections -- or, say better, abusing the election in order to get the results that would suit them. So the role of OSCE was to ensure that the elections were conducted in a most fair and proper way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did their role also include registration of voters?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. OSCE developed procedures for the registration of voters. And, of course, it is not only that they developed procedures, but they were also monitoring how the procedures were followed. So there was a system of registration centres organised in the entire country. Registration centres were covering actually very densely the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina such that voters, eligible voters, could register with ease and that the frequency that the participation rate in the elections could be as high as possible. So they were also involved, OSCE, in preparing the lists of eligible voters. These lists were present in every registration centre in the form of a paper copy and as well in form of a computer database.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So, first, do you know if there were any pre-conditions for people to register to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: In order to be eligible to vote, a person had to be 18 years of age or older at the time of elections. And secondly, the person had to be listed on the 1991 census. That were the pre-conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In order to ensure that the person was on the 1991 census, what did OSCE have to do?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, in order to prove that the person, a person, was on the census, the OSCE actually requested from statistical authorities a copy of the census, actually not of the entire census, but a part of it. The part in which names, date of birth, and JMBG was included. So this was used as the basis for later registering in the election process.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was the act of registering to vote voluntary?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Of course, it was voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Consequently, were there several groups of individual types who were not registered to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, of course. People, for instance, who were too old or too sick or just didn't want to vote, to register and to vote. They are not registered. Only those who were able and who wanted to register to vote are listed in the registers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so since the number of registered voters was not complete, but only a sample, how did that affect your research?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was a sample of the entire population of eligible voters. However, is a very large sample. First of all, the participation rate in 1997 elections, which is the core of the data I worked with, was 88 per cent, almost 90 percent, of eligible voters registered. In terms of an absolute, it is two and a half million individuals who registered to vote. Compared with the size of the 1991 population, as reported in the census, which was 4.4 million, the sample of two and a half million, must be seen as extremely large.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to turn to another subject matter. I wonder if this might be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll rise for today and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of April, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
